summary: Describes Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA), IPv6 addresses whose interface identifier is a hash of a public key and other parameters. This binds the key to the address, which can be verified by recomputing the hash. It is used in Secure Neighbor Discovery.

eli5.summary: Your address is made from a fingerprint of your secret key, so anyone can check that you are really the owner.

questions: what is a cryptographically generated address
how does cga work in ipv6
what is the cga sec parameter
subtitle: IPv6 addresses whose last 64 bits are a hash of the owner's public key, so the address itself proves who owns it.

tldr.problem: On a local IPv6 link, any node can claim any address. Secure Neighbor Discovery needs a way to bind an address to a key without certification authorities or other infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The interface identifier (low 64 bits) is built from a SHA-1 hash of a CGA Parameters structure that holds a modifier, the subnet prefix, a collision count and the public key. A 3-bit Sec value makes generation costlier by forcing extra zero bits in a second hash.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can verify the binding by recomputing the hashes, then check messages signed with the matching private key. An attacker can make new CGAs but cannot take over someone else's. RFC 3972 is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 4581 and RFC 4982.

today: RFC 3972 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 4581 and RFC 4982.

sections.title: Binding a Key to an IPv6 Address
sections.content:
RFC 3972 specifies a way to securely associate a public key with an IPv6 address in Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971). The interface identifier, the rightmost 64 bits of the address, is generated from a cryptographic hash of the public key. The result is a cryptographically generated address (CGA). The matching private key can then sign messages sent from that address.

The document covers how to generate a CGA, how to verify the link between a key and a CGA, and how to sign and verify messages. No public key infrastructure, certification authority or trusted server is needed.

CGAs are not certified. An attacker can create a new CGA from any subnet prefix and any public key, but cannot take a CGA created by someone else and send signed messages that appear to come from its owner.
sections.eli5: Instead of getting an ID card from an office, you make your address out of your own secret stamp. Anyone can check the address matches the stamp, but nobody else can copy your stamp.

sections.title: The CGA Address and Its Security Parameter
sections.content:
A CGA is an IPv6 address with a 64-bit subnet prefix on the left and a 64-bit interface identifier on the right. A three-bit security parameter Sec is encoded in the three leftmost bits of the interface identifier and sets strength against brute-force attacks.

An address is a CGA if two conditions hold. First, Hash1 (64 bits) equals the interface identifier, ignoring bits 0, 1, 2, 6 and 7 (the Sec bits and the "u" and "g" bits). Second, the 16*Sec leftmost bits of Hash2 (112 bits) are zero. With Sec of 0 the second condition is always met; with Sec of 7 the whole 112 bits must be zero.
sections.eli5: Part of the address is a fingerprint of your key. A small dial, Sec, says how many extra zeros your fingerprint had to have, which makes it harder to fake.

sections.title: CGA Parameters and the Two Hashes
sections.content:
Each CGA has a CGA Parameters structure with these fields, in order:

  • Modifier: a 128-bit value that can be anything. It implements the hash extension and adds randomness for privacy.
  • Subnet Prefix: the 64-bit prefix of the CGA.
  • Collision Count: an 8-bit value that MUST be 0, 1 or 2. It is raised to recover from an address collision found by duplicate address detection.
  • Public Key: a DER-encoded ASN.1 SubjectPublicKeyInfo. SEND SHOULD use RSA, with the rsaEncryption identifier, and the key length SHOULD be at least 384 bits.
  • Extension Fields: optional and unused so far. Unrecognized ones MUST be ignored, but still included in the hash input.

Both hashes use SHA-1. Hash1 is the leftmost 64 bits of the SHA-1 of the whole structure. Hash2 is the leftmost 112 bits of the SHA-1 of the same structure with the subnet prefix and collision count set to zero.
sections.eli5: The address is built from a little bundle: a random number, the neighborhood, a counter, and your public key. Squish the bundle into a fingerprint and put the fingerprint in the address.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying a CGA
sections.content:
Generation takes a 64-bit subnet prefix, a public key and a Sec value from 0 to 7. In outline:

  1. Start with a random 128-bit modifier. Hash it with 9 zero octets, the encoded key and any extension fields, and keep the leftmost 112 bits as Hash2.
  2. If the 16*Sec leftmost bits of Hash2 are not all zero, add one to the modifier and repeat. This brute-force search takes O(2^(16*Sec)) iterations.
  3. Set the collision count to 0, hash the full parameters to get Hash1, write Sec into the three leftmost bits and set the "u" and "g" bits to zero, and attach the subnet prefix.
  4. If duplicate address detection finds a collision, increase the collision count and redo the hash; after three collisions, stop and report an error.

Sec of 0 is deterministic and fast, and nodes MAY always use it. If the subnet prefix changes but the key does not, the old modifier MAY be reused, which avoids the costly search but may let an observer link two addresses.

Verification takes the address and the CGA Parameters. It checks that the collision count is 0, 1 or 2, that the prefix matches the address, and that Hash1 matches the interface identifier (ignoring the five masked bits). It then reads Sec and checks that the leading 16*Sec bits of Hash2 are zero. It needs at most two SHA-1 computations and stops at the first failed step. All verifiers MUST handle every Sec value from 0 to 7, and in SEND they SHOULD NOT apply different policy based on Sec.
sections.eli5: Making an address is hard work, like mining for a lucky number. Checking one is quick: just redo the fingerprint and see if it matches.

sections.title: CGA Signatures
sections.content:
To sign a message, a node places a 128-bit type tag from the CGA Message Type name space in front of the message and signs the result with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-1. SEND uses one IANA-allocated, randomly chosen type tag for all its signed messages. The tag is not sent, because the verifier knows it from the ICMP message type.

To verify, the receiver first verifies the CGA, then rebuilds the tagged message and checks the RSA signature with the public key from the CGA Parameters. The verifier MUST accept the signature only if both checks succeed.
sections.eli5: You sign your letters with your secret stamp. A special label on the front says what kind of letter it is, so nobody can reuse your signature on a different kind of letter.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
CGAs prevent stealing and spoofing of existing IPv6 addresses. Impersonation would require a collision in Hash1 (second pre-image resistance). The RFC lists limits: CGAs are not certified, nothing can prove that an address is not a CGA, and the 384-bit minimum RSA key length is short, though costly enough to deter most denial-of-service attacks.

The hash extension exists because 64 bits will not stay enough as computers get faster. Raising Sec multiplies the cost of both generation and brute-force attack by about 2^(16*Sec), while verification cost stays constant. The RFC says Sec values between 0 and 2 are currently sufficient for most IPv6 nodes. Collision counts above 2 are not allowed, because an attacker could try all counts without repeating the modifier search.

For privacy, a host can generate many CGAs using a different random modifier each time, giving pseudonymity comparable to RFC 3041. The public key is revealed in signed messages, so a host wanting pseudonymity should also change keys. To prevent related-protocol attacks, the type tag is prepended to signed messages, and a key used with CGAs MUST be used only for signing, not encryption.
sections.eli5: Nobody can steal your address because they cannot fake your fingerprint. A higher dial setting makes cheating much harder while checking stays just as fast.

sections.title: The CGA Message Type Registry
sections.content: The document creates a CGA Message Type name space of 128-bit unsigned integers for type tags. Values are allocated first come, first served, without review. Requesters SHOULD generate values with a strong random-number generator. Ranges of at most 256 values may be requested if the 120 most significant bits are random. Values for private use MAY be generated without IANA allocation. The document itself defines no new values.
sections.eli5: There is a list of long random label numbers. Anyone can reserve one by asking, as long as they picked it randomly.

viz.caption: FIELDS OF THE CGA PARAMETERS STRUCTURE (RFC 3972)

items.title: Modifier
items.text: 128 bits; searched until Hash2 has enough leading zeros.

items.title: Subnet Prefix
items.text: 64 bits; the prefix of the address.

items.title: Extension Fields
items.text: Optional, variable length; not used yet.

data.title: CGA definition
data.code:
Mask1 = 0x1cffffffffffffff

Hash1 & Mask1  ==  interface identifier & Mask1
Hash2 & Mask2  ==  0x0000000000000000000000000000

Sec = (interface identifier & 0xe000000000000000) >> 61
